title: The Surprising Staying Power of Trump’s Tariffs | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Allison J. Smith argues that, despite widespread affordability anxiety and a plurality believing tariffs raise prices, U.S. public opinion is too split and too partisan to drive a tariff rollback. Even a Democratic midterm win or 2028 White House win is unlikely to produce a significant shift in trade policy; only marginal removals (e.g., on allies or tenuous national-security goods) look plausible.

themes.theme: Affordability anxiety vs. tariff policy preferences

insights.claim: A CFR–Morning Consult survey in August 2026 found 75 percent of U.S. adults are concerned about affording groceries and food, including 46 percent who are very concerned.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Food affordability remains a dominant consumer concern feeding political pressure on prices.
insights.quote: 75 percent of adults are concerned about being able to afford groceries and food products, including 46 percent who are very concerned
insights.locator: Americans across party affiliation are anxious

insights.claim: More than half of U.S. adults surveyed are worried about affording pharmaceuticals and medical supplies.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Healthcare goods price sensitivity makes pharma tariffs politically salient.
insights.locator: Americans across party affiliation are anxious

insights.claim: Only 41 percent of Americans surveyed said the main impact of tariffs is to raise prices, a plurality rather than a majority.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Price-linked anti-tariff sentiment is not broad enough to force policy reversal.
insights.quote: 41 percent of those surveyed said the main impact of tariffs is to raise prices
insights.locator: Americans across party affiliation are anxious

insights.claim: Fewer than 30 percent of Americans want all tariffs removed, 20–24 percent want tariffs limited to national security issues, and around 30 percent support keeping Trump's tariffs or using them as negotiating leverage.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Fragmented preferences mean no clear mandate for wholesale tariff removal; tariff regime likely persists.

insights.claim: Those expecting an overwhelming groundswell of public support for reversing Trump's tariff-forward trade policy are likely to be disappointed.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Investors betting on tariff relief driven by affordability politics should temper expectations.
insights.quote: those expecting an overwhelming groundswell of support for reversing U.S. President Donald Trump

themes.theme: National security as bipartisan tariff justification

insights.claim: Both Republican and Democratic administrations have stretched national security justifications to cover trade exemptions on climate change, public health, energy security, and other issues.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: National-security framing is a durable bipartisan legal and political shield for tariffs.

insights.claim: The Biden administration maintained most of Trump's first-term tariffs and raised Section 301 tariffs on China to support strategic sectors including batteries, critical minerals, EVs, ship-to-shore cranes, solar cells, semiconductors, and steel and aluminum.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: China-focused tariffs on strategic sectors survive changes of party, supporting domestic producers in those industries.

insights.claim: Average U.S. tariffs on Chinese imports were 3.1 percent in January 2018, around 19 percent for most of Biden's term, and 35.2 percent in August 2026.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Tariff levels on China have ratcheted up across administrations, signalling a structural rather than cyclical trend.
insights.quote: U.S. tariffs on Chinese imports were around 19 percent, lower than the 35.2 percent in August 2026 but much higher than the 3.1 percent in January 2018

insights.claim: Americans are more likely to view a good as critical to national security if it has military applications or helps the U.S. compete in emerging high-tech industries, and less likely for public health, manufacturing, or environmental goods.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Tariffs on defense and high-tech goods enjoy firmer public backing than those on manufacturing or green goods.
insights.locator: But national security can be a nebulous

insights.claim: Americans rank energy and medicine as more important to national security than automobiles, computers, and clothing.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Energy and pharma protection is more politically defensible than consumer-goods tariffs, which may be more vulnerable to rollback.
insights.locator: Likewise, Americans view energy and medicine

insights.claim: Americans are comfortable importing essential national security goods from allies such as Canada, Germany, and Japan but less so from China.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Ally-shoring is publicly favored; China-sourced strategic goods face persistent political headwinds.

insights.claim: Support for presidential authority to impose tariffs rises about 10 percentage points among both Democrats and Republicans when the president is from their own party.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Opposition to tariffs is partly partisan and may evaporate under a president of the other party, reducing odds of reversal.
insights.quote: Support for presidential authority to impose tariffs jumps by around 10 percentage points for Democrats and Republicans when the president raising tariffs is from their party
insights.locator: The real contributor to the staying power

insights.claim: Partisanship, rather than national security arguments, may be the real driver of the staying power of U.S. tariffs.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Tariff durability depends on political identity, not policy merits, making it sticky across election cycles.
insights.quote: The real contributor to the staying power of tariffs may end up being partisanship.
insights.locator: The real contributor to the staying power

insights.claim: Even if Democrats win the House or Senate in the 2026 midterms or the White House in 2028, a significant shift in U.S. trade policy is unlikely.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Do not price a broad tariff rollback on a Democratic electoral win; elevated tariffs are a multi-year base case.
insights.quote: there is unlikely to be a significant shift in U.S. trade policy
insights.locator: Next week’s midterms may see a backlash

insights.claim: Some of the more dubious tariffs, such as those on traditional allies like Canada or on goods with tenuous national security links like kitchen cabinets, may be removed.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Selective relief is most likely for ally-sourced and non-strategic goods; Canada-exposed trade could benefit.
insights.locator: Next week’s midterms may see a backlash

insights.claim: Tariffs create constituencies that benefit from them and fight to preserve them, as happened during the Biden administration.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Protected domestic industries become lobbying forces that entrench tariffs, supporting their margins long term.
insights.quote: tariffs also create constituencies that benefit from them and will fight to preserve them
insights.locator: Next week’s midterms may see a backlash

insights.claim: Congress has limited ability to stop a president from imposing tariffs absent a veto-proof majority, even if removing tariffs on allies draws bipartisan support.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Legislative checks on executive tariff power are weak, so tariff policy stays presidential and volatile.
insights.quote: there are limits to what Congress can do to stop the president absent a veto-proof majority
insights.locator: Next week’s midterms may see a backlash

insights.claim: Higher tariffs will likely remain a key feature of U.S. trade policy regardless of which party wins the 2026 midterms.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Plan for persistent tariff-driven cost pressure and supply-chain realignment as the default scenario.
insights.quote: higher tariffs will likely remain a key feature of U.S. trade policy, whichever party prevails in next week’s midterms
insights.locator: Until that happens

insights.claim: Public confusion on tariffs stems from a lack of clarity over alternatives and a lack of political will to change course.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Absent a coherent alternative policy, the tariff status quo remains the path of least resistance.
insights.locator: Ultimately, Americans’ confusion over what to do

insights.claim: Policymakers should consider reforms to existing laws to limit the president's ability to impose tariffs in an aimless fashion.
insights.speaker: Allison J. Smith
insights.so_what: Statutory reform of tariff authority is a longer-dated catalyst to watch for reducing trade-policy volatility.
insights.locator: Ultimately, Americans’ confusion over what to do
